720a743715.q: Why should Nebraska modernize its sales tax base to support income tax reductions?
720a743715.a: Sales tax base broadening is a great opportunity not just because it is a consumption tax, but because there are aspects of consumption that are not taxed where there are things that if you were designing a consumption tax now you would have put them in the base. Shifting toward consumption taxes and away from higher income taxes is better for growth and the state's long-run economy, and it helps sustain income tax reductions with the predictability and stability needed for future policy.

bc95dd7a6d.q: What is the history of sales tax design and why does Nebraska exempt so many services?
bc95dd7a6d.a: The sales tax in the United States begins in Mississippi in 1930 as a Great Depression revenue generator. It is based on the economy at that time and is a goods-based sales tax not capturing services practically at all. Most states including Nebraska start with the idea that goods are in unless exempted but services are only in if expressly added, creating a haphazard system of arbitrary exemptions that have accumulated over six decades rather than being intentionally designed.

5f849b7d55.q: What specific services should Nebraska add to its sales tax base in the first priority tier?
5f849b7d55.a: The first tier includes things like landscaping services, automotive repair labor, laundry and dry cleaning services, household storage, miscellaneous personal services, home maintenance and repair. These are intuitive gaps where you pay sales tax on buying a lawnmower but not on paying someone to cut your lawn weekly, or paying for parts but not labor when getting a car repaired. This first tier would raise about two hundred million dollars a year in state revenue and another fifty two million in local revenue.

395c7c74d1.q: Should Nebraska add motor fuels and groceries to the sales tax base and what are the progressivity concerns?
395c7c74d1.a: Motor fuels are closer to an imperfect user fee than a true consumption tax and many states now tax them as consumption. For groceries, federal law already prevents sales tax on SNAP and WIC purchases, so the exemption primarily benefits higher-income earners. If you reduced the sales tax rate instead of providing the exemption, it would actually be much more progressive for the lowest income households. Research shows the grocery exemption costs over three hundred million dollars a year at the state level and almost eighty million at the local level, with the vast majority of benefit going to upper-income earners.
